subject: physics
title: Kirchhoff's laws and series and parallel circuits
key_idea: Kirchhoff's first law says the currents into a junction equal the currents out, because charge is conserved. His second law says the e.m.f.s round a loop equal the p.d.s, because energy is conserved. Together they give the rules for resistors in series and in parallel.

blocks.text: You must draw and read circuit diagrams using standard symbols.

rows: A long line (positive) and a short line (negative); a battery is two or more cells
A rectangle; a variable resistor has an arrow through it
A circle containing A or V
A gap with a hinged line; a rectangle with a line through it
A triangle pointing in the direction of conventional current, with a bar; an LED has two outward arrows
A resistor rectangle with a diagonal line; an LDR has two inward arrows

Connect a voltmeter in **parallel** across the component.
Ammeters go in series, voltmeters in parallel.
Learn the standard symbols for every component in the syllabus.

blocks.text: The two laws are statements of conservation applied to a circuit.

items.meaning: The sum of the currents entering a junction equals the sum of the currents leaving it.
Round any closed loop, the sum of the e.m.f.s equals the sum of the potential differences.

items: The first law follows from conservation of **charge**. Charge cannot build up at a junction, so what flows in must flow out.
The second law follows from conservation of **energy**. Energy given to each coulomb by the sources equals the energy it transfers in the components.
In dc circuits this means the current is shared out at junctions, and the p.d. is shared out around a loop.
Cells in **series** add their e.m.f.s if they point the same way.
**Identical cells in parallel** give the e.m.f. of one cell, with the current shared between them.
First law: charge is conserved, so current in = current out.
Second law: energy is conserved, so e.m.f. = sum of p.d.s round a loop.

sections.heading: Resistors in series and in parallel

blocks.text: Each rule comes from one of Kirchhoff's laws and from V = IR.

items.text: There are no junctions, so the same current I passes through each resistor.
The supply p.d. is shared: V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃.
IR = IR₁ + IR₂ + IR₃. Divide by I.
Each resistor is connected across the same two points, so each has the same p.d. V.
The supply current splits: I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃.
V/R = V/R₁ + V/R₂ + V/R₃. Divide by V.

items: In series, the total is larger than the largest resistor.
In parallel, the total is smaller than the smallest resistor.
For two resistors in parallel, R = R₁R₂ / (R₁ + R₂).

diagram.alt: Sort statements into those true of series and those true of parallel circuits.
diagram.prompt: Is each statement true of resistors in series or in parallel?

items.text: The same current passes through each resistor
The same p.d. is across each resistor
The p.d.s add up to the supply p.d.
The currents add up to the supply current
The total resistance is larger than any single resistor
The total resistance is smaller than any single resistor

items: Series: current the same, p.d.s add, resistances add.
Parallel: p.d. the same, currents add, reciprocals of resistance add.

blocks.text: For a circuit with series and parallel parts, reduce it step by step, then work back out.

items.text: Replace each parallel group with a single equivalent resistance, then add series resistances.
Use I = E / R for the whole circuit (or the internal resistance too, if given).
Find each p.d. from V = IR, then the current in each branch from I = V / R.
The currents at each junction and the p.d.s round each loop must obey the two laws.

items: Once the currents and p.d.s are known, the power in any part is P = IV = I²R = V²/R.
The energy transferred in a time t is E = IVt.

blocks.text: More than one source of e.m.f.

items.text: Label a current in each branch with an arrow. A wrong guess just gives a negative answer.
Write a current equation at a junction.

Go round each loop in a chosen direction. An e.m.f. counts positive if you go through the cell from − to +. A p.d. IR counts as a fall, so it is negative if you go with the current and positive if you go against it. The terms must sum to zero round the loop.
Solve the simultaneous equations for the unknown currents.

items: Reduce, find the total current, then work back out.
With several sources, write one junction equation and one loop equation per unknown.

checks.q: State Kirchhoff's first law and the conservation law it comes from.
checks.a: The sum of the currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving it. It follows from conservation of charge.

checks.q: Derive the formula for the combined resistance of two resistors in parallel.
checks.a: The p.d. V is the same across each. By the first law I = I₁ + I₂. Since I = V/R, V/R = V/R₁ + V/R₂. Dividing by V gives 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂.

checks.q: A 12 V supply of negligible internal resistance is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6.0 Ω and 12 Ω resistors. Calculate the current from the supply.
